summary_plain: Moves about 51 arcseconds per hour across 13 images over 13.1 hours. Not yet checked against JPL's catalog of known asteroids and comets.

orbit.reported_orbit: The arc is too short to fix one orbit, so this is the most circular of the 1383 sampled orbits that fit the detections; the clones show the range.

known_object.not_checked_reason: JPL Horizons did not answer for 2678 Aavasaksa (1938 DF1), the closest known object (about 10″ away in JPL's quick search).

scores.definition: Rule-based ranking score in [0, 1]: motion_consistency x snr x (1 - artifact_likelihood). It orders candidates for review. It is not a probability.

history.change: linked 13 detections over 3 visits from 2025-10-10 to 2025-10-10

disclaimer: An unmatched candidate may be an imaging artifact, a measurement error, or an object missing from the catalogs we checked. This is not a discovery claim.

thermal.status_plain: Heat detected at 3 SPHEREx channels (at least 3 sigma above reflected sunlight).
thermal.method: Reflected sunlight is modelled from SPHEREx's 0.7-2.6 um reflectance (flux divided by the ASTM E490 solar spectrum), extrapolated to 3.3-5 um and subtracted. The excess is fitted with the Near-Earth Asteroid Thermal Model (NEATM, Harris 1998) with a fixed beaming parameter (1.0 +- 0.2 beyond the near-Earth region, Masiero et al. 2011; 1.4 +- 0.5 for near-Earth objects, Mainzer et al. 2011) and emissivity 0.9; size and albedo are tied through D = 1329 km / sqrt(p_V) x 10^(-H/5). Uncertainties from 400 Monte Carlo draws over flux errors, orbit (or JPL geometry), H, G, beaming parameter and the extrapolation.
thermal.albedo_plain: Bright for an asteroid: reflects about 21% of sunlight, like desert sand.
caveats: Assumes a round asteroid whose heat follows NEATM with beaming parameter 1.0 +- 0.2; a different value moves the size by tens of percent.
Reflected sunlight at 3.3-5 um is extrapolated from 0.7-2.6 um (with a 15% allowance); an unusual surface there would bias the heat.
SPHEREx's channels were measured at different times, so a spinning, elongated asteroid can look brighter in some than others (a 7% allowance per point).
